title: Your Elevator Barely Lifts You: A Hidden Counterweight Does
fb_caption: In most tall buildings, the elevator motor isn't lifting the whole car by itself. Steel ropes run over a grooved wheel at the top to a heavy counterweight that matches the empty car plus about 40 to 50 percent of a full load, so the motor mostly moves the difference. And if a car ever goes too fast, safety brakes clamp onto the rails. Three floors: stairs or elevator?
engagement_comment: Three floors: stairs or elevator? 1 = stairs, always, 2 = elevator, obviously, 3 = depends what I'm carrying.
sources: Wikipedia, Elevator (counterweight typically = cab weight + 40-50% of capacity; steel ropes over a deeply grooved sheave; governor-tripped brake shoes clamp the rails): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator

TK Elevator, Classroom on Demand: Counterweights (cab weight + 40 to 50% of rated load; reduces the effort required by the lifting machine): https://tkelevator.com/us-en/tools/classroom-on-demand/counterweights.html

TK Elevator, Classroom on Demand: Governor (overspeed trips the governor; safety jaws grip the guide rails and stop the cab): https://www.tkelevator.com/us-en/tools/classroom-on-demand/governor-module.html
California Code of Regulations, Title 8 section 1604.15 (counterweight no more than car weight + half the rated load): https://dir.ca.gov/Title8/1604_15.html

tts.director_notes: Calm, knowledgeable American male explainer for a short science/how-it-works social video. Curious and warm, clear and fairly brisk (about 165-180 words per minute), conversational, a short pause before the twist fact, never salesy or dramatic news tone. US English.

beats.text: In most tall buildings, the elevator motor isn't lifting your whole car. A hidden weight is helping.
Your car hangs from steel ropes that loop over a grooved wheel at the top and down to a heavy counterweight.
That counterweight matches the empty car plus about forty to fifty percent of a full load.
So the motor mostly moves the difference, like a seesaw with a friend on the other end.
As your car rises, the counterweight drops, and they pass each other in the shaft.
And if a car ever goes too fast, safety brakes clamp onto the rails and stop it.
Three floors: stairs or elevator? Tell us below.
